build a data warehouse product
## Is your feature request related to a problem? When users scale, data accuracy and reporting flexibility get more important. As a result, they eventually want to export their customer and product data to a warehouse. This happens for two reasons (1) it means they can query a wider range of data together (2) they can debug data issues. This means they will _still_ use PostHog as their data pipeline. However, their business metrics and logic all move to the warehouse too, where they can trust them. We've seen multiple customers in this situation - always higher value ones. This means, however, their value of PostHog is decreased _and_ the customer has a ton of data engineering to do. 2 options: * not care - the market is big enough, so if we lose some revenue because of this, and remain "just a pipeline", we'll be fine * build a warehouse We aren't here to just be fine... ## Describe the solution you'd like We offer customers a data warehouse. It's simpler for them, it's more valuable, and it's all in one. The problems this will solve: * trust in data * keeps product analytics/feature flags/experiments relevant and easy to use forever - in fact it'd make them _more_ powerful * no need to set up complex data stack * no need to hire data engineers *but* is compatible with them * gradual on ramp to a warehouse versus rip 'n replace - we've a ton of potential distribution and can actually win Customers will need: * _Data in_ Need Revenue/production database/CRM data * Stripe / po

Make it easier to separate different websites
## Is your feature request related to a problem? It's currently impossible to separate web and app traffic in some cases. If they are on different hosts (domain or subdomain), this is relatively simple to do with the Host filter (and will help), but if the structure is something like... Marketing pages: Product ...then this is harder to do. If there were only a few pages one could use a regex, but this approach does not work if there are many pages. In this example, the marketing pages and the product could be completely separate sites, that are combined into the same subdomain using e.g. cloudflare. We should also consider how the breakdowns should look, e.g. whether Top paths should just be the pathname, or whether we should include the full url. ## Describe the solution you'd like ```javascript // in the marketing site posthog.init( "SOME_API_KEY", { site_name: "marketing_site" } ) ``` ```javascript // in the product site posthog.init( "SOME_API_KEY", { site_name: "product_site" } ) ``` ```javascript // in the iOS app posthog.init( "SOME_API_KEY", { site_name: "ios_app" } ) ``` The API key is the same, as these are in the same project, so funnels etc work. The `site_name` would get passed as a property with all events, and appears in in-sights and web analytics as a built-in property. It could be pretty useful to have this as a built-in property for other reasons too, e.g. this would be useful as a filter in many trends, and it would be potentially useful to show users the

HogQL wire compatibility with postgres
## Is your feature request related to a problem? I want to be able to use existing tools I'm familiar with to easily plug into the PostHog data warehouse and run HogQL queries. Things like BI tools (metabase), ETL tools, DBT, my own product etc. This way we can instantly plug PostHog into many different tools, without having to build all of them ourselves. I know @mariusandra had built a JDBC type connector on the way to Aruba, but JDBC is much less supported than the Postgres wire protocol. ## Describe the solution you'd like A host that I can connect to with any Postgres client, using something like (or something we roll ourselves) and run HogQL queries against. Support for basic pg_schema type queries, like getting a list of tables. At some point, perhaps support for creating tables, inserting data etc, but all further away. I think there would be some benefit to also getting our SQL dialect closer to Postgres SQL Dialact (or use sqlglot), but thats not necessary for this to work. ## Describe alternatives you've considered ## Additional context #### *Thank you* for your feature request – we love each and every one!

HogQL unnecessary ifNull sets cause slow queries
## In what situation are you experiencing subpar performance? ``` sql select toDate(timestamp) as timestamp, count() from events where timestamp >= addDays(today(), -10) group by timestamp limit 100 ``` The above HogQL will be replaced with something like this Clickhouse sql ```sql SELECT toDate(toTimeZone(events.timestamp, %(hogql_val_0)s), %(hogql_val_1)s) AS timestamp, count() FROM events WHERE and(equals(events.team_id, 3), ifNull(greaterOrEquals(timestamp, addDays(today(), -10)), 0)) GROUP BY timestamp LIMIT 100 SETTINGS readonly=2, max_execution_time=600, allow_experimental_object_type=1, format_csv_allow_double_quotes=0, max_ast_elements=1000000, max_expanded_ast_elements=1000000, max_query_size=524288 ``` In this scenario, there is no need to wrap `ifNull` on the outer layer of 'timestamp'. If the amount of data is large enough, executing this SQL requires huge extra overhead. ## How to reproduce HogQL Debug ## Environment - [x] PostHog Cloud - [x] PostHog self-hosted with Kubernetes (deprecated, see ["Sunsetting Kubernetes support"]( version/commit: [please provide] ## Additional context At the same time, will other fields like timestamp have the same problem? #### *Thank you* for your performance issue report – we want PostHog to go supersonic!

Error tracking
The Replay team are working on a new Error tracking product within PostHog. In helping customers to build more successful products one of the most common requests we get is whether I can watch sessions of users who've encountered errors. A big part of the reason people request this is that they want to identify and resolve the most important issues their customers face, whether that be because it occurs frequently, affects a VIP customer or happened during the checkout flow. Network response status and speed, Errors, Events, and Replay overlap to give a full picture of what's happening in the user's app. Given PostHog already captures so much context about user sessions it makes total sense to integrate an exception tracking product that can compliment our existing user filtering and session replay. Our first version will include: - SDK support to capture errors in one front-end and one back-end language (almost certainly JS and Python). Including autocapture - Stack traces are actionable and human-readable (un-minifying / source map uploading) - Grouping of similar exceptions and errors - High-volume or high-value errors trigger the Alerting system - Advanced user filtering - Integrated with other products and features including as Session replay, Product analytics and Discussions The [Replay Team]( is actively working on this and we'd love to hear user feedback, as well as ideas for features or stretch goals. Please add to this issue! If you like this idea, please leave a 👍

Improve cookieless tracking
### Feature request ## Is your feature request related to a problem? Our previous iteration of cookieless tracking is linked here: It works by storing the data that would go in the cookie, in memory instead, which means it's lost on a page reload. ## Describe the solution you'd like The state-of-the-art approach to cookieless tracking is creating a privacy-preserving hash server-side, using some properties, e.g., user agent, IP address, hostname, and a daily salt. No PII is stored, as the daily salt is thrown away, so it'd be impossible to reverse-engineer a user's identity from a hash. ## Describe alternatives you've considered We could keep our current approach of doing things in memory. ## Additional context There's a lot of details to get right: * How does this work at the API level? Do clients in this mode leave the distinct ID blank, which would be replaced server-side by the hash? * How do session IDs work? As this is stateless, we wouldn't have a way of rolling a new session only after 30 minutes of activity, without adding additional state. * How often does the hash need to rotate? Daily is common, could users customize this setting? * What other docs do we need? Presumably, people would use this mode because they don't have cookie consent, do we need to add docs saying not to send other PII in this mode? * How does the upgrade path work when cookie consent is given?

Saving as view shouldn't require aliasing every field
Right now, to save a query as a view, you need to alias every field. This was a workaround in making it easy for field identification for MVP. This should actually just work by inferring the name of the field. If the field is a transformation (functions are applied on the field), only then return a syntax error/note and prompt the user to name that field.

Move remaining batch exports (S3, Snowflake) to SPMC model
BigQuery and Redshift batch exports now operate in a spmc (single-produce multiple-consumers) model. This model has ensured good throughput and ensuring our connection stays in use, while being reliable enough to survive retries (thanks to only being a single producer). We should expand the model to S3 and Snowflake too, also so that all batch exports are aligned.

Event-property conditional recording
### Feature request ## Is your feature request related to a problem? Teams need a way to start (or limit) session recordings based on event and pageview properties directly in the UI, without code changes or deployments. Current controls (sampling, static URL matching, feature flags by person/cohort) don’t let us target recordings to granular, real-time conditions present on $pageview or other events. This is especially painful for high-traffic projects that purposely only send $pageview (with rich properties) to keep data simple and costs down. ## Describe the solution you'd like A **UI rule builder** for recordings that lets you define **event-driven conditions**: - **When to start recording** - Trigger when an event matches conditions, e.g.: - Event: `$pageview` - Properties: - `iframed` **is** `true` - `org_feature_flags` **contains** `express_checkout_v2` - `org_prop_country` **is** `uk` - `org_name` **is** `mikes_world` - **Where the rule applies** - Choose project-wide, specific domains, or environment (prod/staging). - **Cost controls** - Optional sampling on top of the rule (e.g., record 10% of matching sessions). - Daily/weekly caps and “stop when N sessions captured”. - **Timing semantics** - Default: **start recording from the first matching event onward** in the session. - Optional: if a session already exists when the rule first matches, begin recording **from that moment** (no retroactive capture). - **Manageability** - Create/enable/disable rules from the UI.

### Bug Description ## Bug description Pinned properties in the session replay overview reset to defaults when navigating away from the replays page and returning. The user's customizations are lost even though they were saved to localStorage. **Root cause:** kea-localstorage only reads from localStorage during the BUILD phase of a logic. Since `sessionRecordingPinnedPropertiesLogic` is a singleton (non-keyed), its build is cached and reused on subsequent mounts. When the logic remounts, it skips the build phase (cache hit) and initializes Redux state from `logic.defaults` - which still contains the value from the **first build** (before user customization), not the updated localStorage value. **The flow:** 1. First visit: logic builds, localStorage is empty → `logic.defaults` = hardcoded defaults 2. User pins properties → localStorage updated correctly 3. Navigate away → logic unmounts, but build cache retained with stale `logic.defaults` 4. Return → logic reused from cache (no rebuild) → Redux initializes from stale defaults **Key files:** - `frontend/src/scenes/session-recordings/player/player-meta/sessionRecordingPinnedPropertiesLogic.ts` - kea-localstorage reads localStorage in `persistReducer` during build only ## How to reproduce 1. ### Bug Description ## Problem Customer was using `posthog-python` to call `get_all_flags` with local evaluation enabled. This was working fine and dandy. However, later, they created a Survey on PostHog.com. Little did they know, that surveys are backed by a system created feature flag. This feature flag uses an operator `is_not_set` which is NOT supported by local evaluation. When evaluating a flag locally that cannot be evaluated locally, local evaluation falls back to making a `/flags` request to evaluate a flag. So suddenly, this customer is making a lot of requests they weren't expecting. This is surprising behavior. Feature flag testing
### What is feature flag testing? Feature flag testing lets you preview how a feature flag will behave before it affects real users. Think of it as a "what if" simulator for your flags. **This should be a built-in tool within the PostHog app** (e.g., accessible from the feature flag detail page), not a standalone external tool. The value comes from having direct access to PostHog's flag evaluation logic, existing person/cohort data, and flag version history. I'm not sure where _exactly_ in the product it should live (or if it should be accessible from multiple places), but the idea is that I want users to be able to build a flag in the UI and then test it against real users, groups, cohorts, etc. **The problem**: Testing feature flag behavior today typically means serving them to real users. - **Validating conditions requires real traffic**: You configured the flag to match against a cohort of internal users, but the only way to confirm it works is to wait for someone to trigger it. - **Debugging can feel like guesswork**: A user reports seeing the wrong variant, but you can't easily replicate what properties they had or why the flag evaluated that way. - **Complex behaviors are hard to verify**: Things like experience continuity ensure consistent variants across anonymous and identified sessions, but understanding how changes in distinct ID affect flag evaluation can be opaque. - **Comparing changes is manual**: Users are evaluating unexpectedly after last week's flag update

use ClickHouse subquery for filtered clustering sampling
## Context When `trace_filters` are set for clustering, `fetch_eligible_trace_ids` samples trace IDs from the `events` table, then passes them as an `IN (...)` clause to the `raw_document_embeddings` table. This is inefficient because most filtered events don't have embeddings — we currently oversample by 50x to compensate (PR #47864). ## Proposal Replace the two-step fetch with a single ClickHouse subquery that joins events with embeddings server-side: ```sql SELECT document_id, embedding, rendering FROM raw_document_embeddings WHERE ... AND document_id IN ( SELECT DISTINCT properties.$ai_trace_id FROM events WHERE event IN ('$ai_span', '$ai_generation', ...) AND <property_filters> AND timestamp >= ... AND timestamp < ... ) ORDER BY rand() LIMIT {max_samples} ``` HogQL supports this — `parse_select()` accepts `SelectQuery` AST nodes as placeholders (see `hogql_cohort_query.py` for the pattern). ## Benefits - Eliminates the 50x oversample multiplier and large `IN (...)` clause (up to 75K items) - ClickHouse handles the join efficiently with its column-oriented engine - Exact results — no risk of undershooting the target sample size - Works for both trace-level and generation-level (generation needs a two-hop join: events -> trace_ids -> generation UUIDs -> embeddings) ## Files - `posthog/temporal/llm_analytics/trace_clustering/data.py` — `fetch_eligible_trace_ids` and `fetch_item_embeddings_for_clustering` ## References - Current fix (Option B): #47864 - HogQL subquery patter

Treat explicitly-provided null properties as locally evaluatable
## Context When evaluating feature flags locally, the SDK currently treats a property with a `null` value the same as a missing property — both result in the flag being considered "not locally evaluatable," returning `None`. This conflates two semantically different cases: 1. **Property key is absent** — the caller doesn't know the value → not locally evaluatable → `None` (correct) 2. **Property key is present but value is `null`** — the caller is asserting the value is null → should be locally evaluatable → evaluate normally → `true` or `false` ## Proposal Change the local evaluation logic so that if a property key is present in the provided properties dict (i.e. `"key" in dict`), it's treated as locally evaluatable — even if the value is `null`. Only treat a flag as not locally evaluatable when the required property key is entirely absent from the request. This is a natural contract between caller and library: if I bother to include the key, I'm telling you I know the value. ## Why this matters Currently, if a flag has a release condition on a property like `plan`, and the caller passes `{ plan: null }`, the SDK returns `None` instead of evaluating the condition. If the value is an object with a numeric `total` property, replace the property value with that number and continue processing instead of dropping. # Behavioral cohorts event backfilling mega-issue ## Part 1: How Person Property Backfilling Works for Realtime Cohorts ### Current state of affairs PostHog has **two complementary systems** that power realtime cohort evaluation: 1. **Realtime cohort membership calculation** -- a Temporal scheduled workflow that periodically recomputes which persons are in/out of each realtime cohort by querying `precalculated_events` and `precalculated_person_properties` tables, then writing membership diffs to `cohort_membership`. 2. **Precalculated person properties backfill** -- a one-time Temporal workflow (triggered via management command or admin UI) that evaluates person property filter bytecodes against every person in a team and writes results to the `precalculated_person_properties` ClickHouse table. The **missing piece** is an analogous backfill for *event data*. The `precalculated_events` table is populated in real-time by the `CdpPrecalculatedFiltersConsumer` Node.js consumer, which evaluates behavioral filter bytecodes against incoming events from `KAFKA_EVENTS_JSON`. But there is **no backfill mechanism** for historical events -- if a new cohort is created with behavioral filters, only events arriving *after* the cohort creation get evaluated and written to `precalculated_events`. inject governor Clock to make rate-limit tests deterministic
## Background PR #55399 fixed a 100% test failure rate on Blacksmith CI runners for the `rust/feature-flags` rate-limit tests. The root cause is that `governor`'s default `QuantaClock` is TSC-backed, and TSC calibration differs across hypervisors (Blacksmith vs Depot), causing the token bucket to replenish faster than wall-clock seconds. The test-only fix in #55399 widens the rate-limit windows (`1/second` → `1/minute`) so that wall-clock waits dominate any TSC drift. It ships real-time `sleep`s up to 11 seconds, which is a reasonable CI cost but leaves two things unresolved: 1. The tests are still non-deterministic in principle. They rely on real elapsed wall-clock time rather than a controllable clock. 2. Production code uses the default `QuantaClock` by construction, so any production rate limiter with sub-minute granularity has the same TSC exposure on the same hypervisors. For per-minute-or-longer windows this is noise, but worth auditing. ## Proposed approach `governor` supports injecting a `Clock` when constructing a `RateLimiter`, and ships a `FakeRelativeClock` explicitly for tests. Introducing a clock seam lets tests be fully deterministic (advance the clock instantly) and removes wall-clock sleeps from the suite. Rough shape: ```rust pub struct FlagsRateLimiter<C: Clock = QuantaClock> { inner: RateLimiter<SomeKey, SomeState, C>, } impl<C: Clock> FlagsRateLimiter<C> { pub fn new_with_clock(quota: Quota, clock: C) -> Self { ... } } // tests let clock = FakeRelativeCl

MCP `create-feature-flag` and `update-feature-flag` can't set `is_remote_configuration`
## Problem The `create-feature-flag` and `update-feature-flag` MCP tools don't expose `is_remote_configuration`, so agents can't create or convert a flag into Remote Config mode through the MCP. - `create-feature-flag` always creates flags with `is_remote_configuration: false`. - `update-feature-flag` can't flip an existing flag into Remote Config mode. - The only workaround is a manual toggle in the PostHog UI, which defeats the point of managing flags through the MCP. The field is read-exposed: `feature-flag-get-definition` returns `is_remote_configuration: <bool>` on any flag. It's settable in the UI and the Django serializer (`posthog/api/feature_flag.py`) lists it among writable fields. It's just unreachable through the MCP write tools. ## Where it lives `products/feature_flags/mcp/tools.yaml` has explicit `include_params` allowlists for both tools that omit `is_remote_configuration`: ```yaml create-feature-flag: operation: feature_flags_create ... include_params: - key - name - filters - active - tags - evaluation_contexts update-feature-flag: operation: feature_flags_partial_update ... include_params: - key - name - filters - active - tags - evaluation_contexts ``` The generated `services/mcp/src/tools/generated/feature_flags.ts` only copies those six fields into the request body, so `is_remote_configuration` never reaches the API even if a caller supplies it. ## Suggested fix Add `is_remote_configuration` to both `include_params` lists in `tools.yaml` and regenerate.

### Feature request Currently, PostHog experiments only support upper/lower bound percentile filtering for outlier management across all exposed users. This creates issues when analyzing metrics for features with low adoption rates. For example, with 10,000 exposures per variant but only 80-50 users actually using the feature, setting percentile bounds at 99% filters out the actual feature users rather than just outliers. This makes it impossible to get meaningful percentile metrics (P50/P75/P90) for the subset of users who engaged with the feature. Describe the solution you'd like Add support for percentile metrics (P50, P75, P90, P95, P99) in experiment results that can be calculated specifically for users who performed the target action, rather than across all exposed users. This would allow filtering outliers within the engaged user subset, providing more accurate statistical analysis for features with low conversion rates. Describe alternatives you've considered Currently using upper/lower bound percentiles at 99.9%, but this doesn't solve the core issue when feature usage is very low relative to total exposures. Manual HogQL queries could potentially calculate these metrics, but this requires significant technical overhead and doesn't integrate with the experiment UI. Experiment metric precomputation failures are silently masked by the direct-path fallback
## Background Follow-up from review of [#60380]( which fixed an unconditional `toUInt8(...)` failure in the funnel events precomputation INSERT (`experiment_metric_events_preaggregated`). That bug had been failing **every** matching INSERT in production (deterministically, ~3.8k warns/24h) yet wasn't surfacing as a user-visible problem. The reason: there is a fallback path — when precomputation fails, the query runner falls back to the "direct" path and still returns results. So a complete, deterministic failure of the precomputation path was effectively invisible. ## Problem The fallback is good for resilience, but it masks errors. A precomputation path can be 100% broken and we'd never notice because results keep coming back via the direct path — just slower and without the precomputation benefit. We only caught this one because of the log noise. ## What we should do - **Make these errors propagate / surface.** A precomputation failure shouldn't be silently swallowed by the fallback — it should be observable (alerting, error reporting, or surfaced metrics) so we know when the precomputation path is broken even though the fallback keeps queries working. - **Improve observability** around the precomputation vs. direct path — e.g. track how often the fallback is being hit and why, so a systematic failure stands out instead of blending into normal retry noise. (Discussed further in the Slack thread.) cc @lricoy

bug(flags):Orphaned person profiles created via $feature_flag_called event
## Summary Every server-side SDK auto-fires a `$feature_flag_called` event when you evaluate a flag with a `distinct_id`, and none of them mark that event as personless (`$process_person_profile = false`). Ingestion treats an event as personful whenever a `distinct_id` is present and nothing says otherwise, so any `distinct_id` that has no other events ends up with a person profile created from the flag-called event alone. You see this most with backend services that evaluate flags across a large or short-lived set of `distinct_id`s. Those IDs never send a `pageview` or `identify`, so the flag-called event is the only thing that ever creates their profile. The result is a pile of empty, orphaned profiles that cost storage and person volume but tell you nothing. ## How profiles get created today Ingestion defaults an event to personful and only backs off when `$process_person_profile` is explicitly `false`: - `nodejs/src/ingestion/event-processing/normalize-process-person-flag-step.ts:29` sets `let processPerson = true // The default.` - Only a literal `false` (or the `force_disable_person_processing` header) turns it off (same file, lines 37-43). So a `$feature_flag_called` event with a `distinct_id` and no `$process_person_profile=false` is personful, and `processPersonsStep` creates or updates a person even when the event carries no `$set` properties at all. ## Cross-SDK status No server SDK sets `$process_person_profile=false` on the auto-fired `$feature_flag_called` event

Copying a flag across projects doesn't copy its flag dependencies
### Background #64472 fixes the hard-fail that happened when copying a flag with a flag-to-flag dependency across projects. The fix is deliberately conservative: when copying flag A that depends on flag B, it remaps the dependency to B in the target project if an active B already exists there, and otherwise drops the dependency, warns the user, and forces the copied flag inactive so a now-ungated condition group can't roll out to everyone. That's the right behavior for a bugfix, but it leaves a gap: the copy never offers to bring B along. If B doesn't already exist (or is disabled) in the target project, the user has to notice the warning, manually copy B first, then re-copy A. Nothing guides them toward that. ### Proposal Offer to copy a flag's dependencies as part of the cross-project copy, ideally as an explicit opt-in rather than implicit recursion, e.g. "Copy these flags and their N dependencies?" so the user stays in control of what gets written. ### Design questions to settle - **Transitive dependencies** — B depends on C depends on D. How deep do we resolve? - **Cycles** — A and B depending on each other needs detection. - **Overwrite semantics** — if a flag with B's key already exists in the target but differs (the disabled-B case #64472 deliberately refuses to enable), do we touch it? - **B's own baggage** — cohorts to remap, payloads, schedules, B's own `active` state. - **Partial failure** — if A copies but B fails, what state are we left in? ### Out of scope here

verify-and-fix logs SoftTimeLimitExceeded as "Error fixing cache"
### Problem In the periodic flags hypercache verify-and-fix task, `_fix_and_record` wraps the cache write in a broad `except Exception` (`posthog/storage/hypercache_verifier.py`, around L307-316): ```python try: if "db_data" in verification: config.hypercache.set_cache_value(team, verification["db_data"]) success = True else: success = config.update_fn(team) except Exception as e: success = False logger.exception("Error fixing cache", team_id=team.id, issue_type=issue_type, error=str(e)) ``` Celery's `SoftTimeLimitExceeded` subclasses `Exception`, so when the soft time limit fires while a fix is mid-write (for example inside a boto3 `put_object` to object storage), it is caught here and logged as `Error fixing cache`. Two problems: 1. It is misleading. The write didn't fail for a cache or storage reason; the run simply ran out of time. These surface as error-level logs and inflate the apparent fix-failure rate. 2. It can swallow the wind-down signal. `SoftTimeLimitExceeded` is meant to tell the task to stop gracefully. Catching it per-team and continuing the loop defeats that, letting the run keep going toward the hard limit instead of winding down. This is most visible during a large fix burst, e.g. after a new field is added to the flags cache payload, when the next verify run must rewrite every team's entry and a run can approach the soft time limit. ### Suggested fix Handle `SoftTimeLimitExceeded` (and `TimeLimitExceeded`) explicitly before the broad `except Exception` an

"Fixing cache entry" info logs flood and get relabeled error during fix bursts
### Problem The flags hypercache verify-and-fix task logs one INFO `Fixing cache entry` line per fixed team (`posthog/storage/hypercache_verifier.py:305`), with no cap or sampling. During a large fix burst, e.g. after a new field is added to the flags cache payload, when the next verify run rewrites every team's entry, this emits a very large number of identical-shape info lines from a single run in a few minutes. Separately, these `Fixing cache entry` entries were observed in Loki with `level=error` even though the JSON body reads `"level": "info"`. That points to a stdout/stderr routing or pipeline relabeling issue: info logs landing on stderr get promoted to an error label. Combined with the per-team volume above, a legitimate fix burst can spike the apparent error rate and risk tripping false-positive error-rate alerts. ### Suggested fix 1. Reduce per-team log volume during bursts: cap or sample the per-team `Fixing cache entry` info log, or aggregate into a periodic summary (e.g. "fixed N teams so far") instead of one line per team. 2. Investigate the stderr routing so INFO logs are not relabeled `level=error`. ### Impact Low severity, observability only. No functional effect, but the log volume plus error relabeling can produce misleading error-rate signals and alert noise during legitimate large fix passes.

Decide the repair contract for membership transitions lost between state commit and produce
The cohort stream processor commits evaluation state to RocksDB first, then produces the resulting membership transitions to Kafka, and advances consumer offsets only after the produce succeeds. A produce failure holds the offset so the event replays, but the replay evaluates against the already committed state, sees no flip, and never emits the transition again. A crash between the state commit and the produce loses the transition the same way. Two sweep code paths additionally drop their output on produce failure on purpose (`rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/workers/worker.rs`). That was acceptable while the output was a shadow topic nobody consumed. Build mark and sweep deletion in the CDP cohort membership consumer
When a cohort definition is edited, a reconcile run replays the cohort's full current membership as a snapshot tagged with a run id, then emits one completion marker per processor partition on the dedicated `cohort_reconcile_markers` topic. The CDP membership consumer today only upserts (`nodejs/src/cdp/consumers/cdp-cohort-membership.consumer.ts`). Live transitions flip `in_cohort`, but a person who no longer matches an edited definition gets no live transition and no snapshot message, so their row stays `in_cohort = true` in the `cohort_membership` Postgres table forever. The designed fix is mark and sweep: once every completion marker for a run has arrived, remove the rows for that cohort whose version is older than the run. This was designed but never built or exercised. Building it needs four pieces: parse the `run_id` field the processor already emits instead of discarding it, add a version column to the `cohort_membership` table, consume the marker topic, and run the sweep once all markers for a run have arrived.

All membership evaluation state lives in RocksDB on a single pod's local volume. Losing that volume today means rerunning backfills, which is annoying but harmless because nothing consumes the output yet. The processor has an S3 checkpoint and restore layer, but it is off by default (`CHECKPOINT_ENABLED` in `rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/config.rs`), has never run in production, and no bucket or access role is provisioned. There is no periodic full upload, so a checkpoint can reference arbitrarily old files and a bucket retention policy would delete files a restore still needs, silently breaking recovery. A failed restore logs a warning and cold starts with an empty store instead of alerting. Enabling checkpoints without configuring a bucket silently does nothing. There is no metric for bytes uploaded, so cost cannot be sized. Fix the defects, provision the bucket and access, then run a restore drill and verify that a pod restored from S3 serves correct membership.

prompt fetches rate limited like feature flag local evaluation

create the pipeline Kafka topics
The pipeline topics do not exist in EU. **Action** Create these topics on the EU ingestion Kafka cluster, with the same partition counts and retention as prod-us: `cohort_stream_events`, `person_merge_events`, `cohort_merge_state_transfer`, `cohort_cascade_events`, `cohort_stream_seed_events`, `cohort_reconcile_markers`, `cohort_membership_changed`, `cohort_membership_changed_shadow`. This comes first. The stream processor, the seeder and ingestion refuse to start when a topic they use is missing. The membership consumer reads nothing from a missing topic and reports no error. **Done when** all eight topics exist in EU with the prod-us partition counts. **Depends on** #107985

add the event shuffler's read-only database user

move the cohort membership consumer to the ingestion Kafka cluster
In EU, `cdp-cohort-membership-consumer` still reads the legacy Kafka cluster. Its sweeper is off, and its resources are smaller than in prod-us. **Action** - Point the consumer at the ingestion cluster. - Turn the sweeper on. - Apply the prod-us autoscaling and resources. - Include EU in the consumer's crash alert, which excludes EU today. **Done when** the consumer and the sweeper run on the ingestion cluster in EU with no restarts. **Depends on** #107986

emit person merge events from ingestion
The stream processor moves cohort state when persons merge, and it learns of merges from `person_merge_events`. deploy cohort-event-shuffler
**Action** Deploy `cohort-event-shuffler` to EU with the prod-us configuration. Set its team allowlist to PostHog's EU project. Set the allowlist explicitly. deploy cohort-stream-processor
**Action** - Deploy `cohort-stream-processor` to EU with the prod-us configuration: cascade, durable restore, seed apply and reconcile, storage guards, resources and disk size. - Set its team allowlist explicitly to PostHog's EU project. - Give its volume the same claim name as prod-us, so the existing disk alert and dashboards cover it. **Done when** - The processor passes its startup checks. - It emits membership changes for the EU project. - The membership consumer writes those changes. **Depends on** #107988, #107989

configure feature flags for realtime membership, reads off

Add one access record per team in Postgres, and give it an API for staff. 2. Make every service read it. The shuffler, the processor and the seeder already poll Postgres for cohort definitions. 3. Granting access starts the team's backfills. Revoking access stops processing for the team. 4. Remove the environment lists. **Done when** enabling a team is one write with no deploy, and every service gives the same answer for the same team.

Users turn it on from the cohort page, or from the flag editor when they pick a cohort. 2. The processor and the seeder load only enabled cohorts. Turning a cohort on starts its backfill and shows the existing "preparing" state. 3. Refuse to turn a cohort off while a flag or an active workflow reads it. The workflows cohort lock from #117007 does this for edits already. 4. Person-only cohorts that only flags read do not need it. Flags evaluate person properties directly. 5. Cohorts that pilot projects use today stay enabled. 6. Capture an event when a user turns realtime on or off. **Done when** a user enables a cohort with no operator step, and the pipeline reads, stores and backfills nothing for cohorts that are not enabled. **Depends on** #120356

Realtime cohorts need two limits: how many cohorts a project enables, and how much history a cohort backfills. The limits that exist today act without telling the user. **Today** - The seeder caps history at `SEEDER_MAX_LOOKBACK_DAYS`, 400 days by default (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/domain/plan.rs`). A cohort with a longer window gets truncated history. The run row gets a `LookbackTruncated` note, and the cohort still reads as ready. - A cohort over `REALTIME_COHORT_MAX_PERSON_COUNT` loses its realtime type on the next daily calculation. - Nothing limits how many cohorts a project enables. **Action** 1. Add a limit on enabled cohorts per project and a limit on history length, with values set per plan. 2. Check the history limit at save time, for relative windows and for absolute start dates. Refuse with a reason instead of truncating. 3. When a project goes over a limit, freeze the cohorts over it instead of switching them off. A frozen cohort keeps its last membership and stops updating. Cohorts that a flag or workflow reads freeze last. 4. A frozen cohort resumes, with a backfill, once it fits again. For a new team, an operator runs `create_cohort_backfill_run`. - Each save-triggered run plans its own day range. A burst of saves, such as a bulk resave, queues one run per cohort and repeats the same scans. - A person-property run scans every person on the team. - The seeder claims chunks by day and band across all runs, with no fairness between teams (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/store/chunks.rs`). **Action** 1. A backfill run reconciles each of its cohorts and records an outcome for each one. When an outcome is missing and the error is retryable, nothing repairs the run without an operator. **Today** - The Django finalizer holds the run in `reconciling` and treats the shortfall as one that "simply holds until re-dispatch" (`products/cohorts/backend/backfill/finalize.py`). - The seeder's auto-dispatch re-dispatches only runs with no usable dispatch record (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/app/completion.rs`). - Completion discovery skips runs that already carry `reconcile_observed_at` (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/store/completion.rs`). - So the run waits for an operator to run `reconcile_dispatch`. mask the identity verification secret by default
## What happens On **Support → Settings → General**, the **Identity verification secret** field shows the full secret in plain text as soon as the page loads. You don't have to click "reveal". So anything that sees the page can read the secret: - a screen share - a screenshot - a browser automation or AI agent reading the page - someone looking over your shoulder You only need to open the settings to change something unrelated, such as a widget domain or the Slack channel. That is when it gets exposed. We hit this twice in one afternoon. Both times an assistant was changing unrelated Support settings for us. It read or screenshotted the page, the secret ended up in its transcript, and we had to rotate the secret each time. (The rotate + "Expire now" flow is good, thank you. It's just needed more often than it should be.) ## Suggestion - **Masking:** mask the secret by default (`••••••••abcd`, last 4 characters at most), with a reveal or copy button. - **Copying:** the copy button should copy the full value without showing it, as the Stripe and GitHub token pages do. - **Accessible text:** keep the full value out of the page's text and accessibility tree until it's revealed, so agents that read the DOM don't pick it up. - **Other secrets:** the same treatment may suit any other secret shown in project settings. ## Environment - PostHog Cloud EU - Support (Conversations) settings page, November 2026

SDK local evaluation matches person_metadata cohort filters against the caller's created_at property
## Bug Description Since #62230, a cohort can filter on Person metadata > First seen (`type: "person_metadata"`, `key: "created_at"`). `/flags` reads that value from the persons table and ignores any `created_at` person property ([flag_matching_utils.rs#L547]( SDK local evaluation gets this wrong. The definitions endpoint sends the cohort filter unchanged ([local_evaluation.py#L770]( Most SDKs treat every filter type other than `cohort` and `flag` as a person property, so they match the filter against a `created_at` key in the person properties the caller passes. For a flag that targets such a cohort: - If the caller doesn't pass `created_at`, the SDK returns inconclusive and falls back to `/flags`. That's correct. - If the caller passes a `created_at` person property, the SDK returns a result based on that value instead of the person's real creation time, so it can disagree with `/flags`. #62230 mentions that some teams set their own `created_at` person property. ## How to reproduce With posthog-python at 933c3c7, create a flag whose only condition is a cohort with `{"type": "person_metadata", "key": "created_at", "operator": "is_date_after", "value": "2025-01-01"}` and evaluate it locally: - `person_properties={}` returns inconclusive. - `person_properties={"created_at": "2026-06-01"}` returns `True`. - `person_properties={"created_at": "2020-06-01"}` returns `False`. `/flags` returns the same answer in all three cases because it uses the person's actual `created_at`. ## Af

error tracking - choose which exception properties show by default
## Is your feature request related to a problem? On an error tracking issue's Properties tab, the default table shows a fixed list of built-in properties plus a "Custom properties" section with the properties whose names don't start with `$`. Every other property is only visible after switching on the JSON toggle, which shows all properties on the event, unfiltered. To see a few specific `$` properties, or to read nested values such as job arguments or request params, users have to switch to the full JSON view and search through it. ## Describe the solution you'd like The requester suggested a single properties view that always renders values as rich JSON (nested values expandable), filtered by default to the same properties the table shows today, with the JSON toggle becoming a "Show all" option. They would also like to choose which properties show by default, per project. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Switch on the JSON toggle and use the "Filter properties" box, which also filters the JSON view by property name. - Copy `$` properties to names without the `$` in SDK code (for example in a `before_send` callback) so they show under "Custom properties". The requester found this heavy, because the data is already on the event. - Add rows to the hardcoded built-in list, as #135312 (Rails job properties) and #136644 (request method, path, and user agent) did. This covers specific SDK properties, but a project cannot choose its own. ## Additional context From: Wher
